title: YOU CAN STARE AT YOUR FAILURES FOR THE REST OF YOUR LIFE… AND STILL NEVER BECOME HOLY.
paragraphs: YOU CAN STARE AT YOUR FAILURES FOR THE REST OF YOUR LIFE… AND STILL NEVER BECOME HOLY.
“Fixing Our Eyes on Jesus” — The Hidden Power of Hebrews 12, and Why Your Greatest Spiritual Breakthrough May Begin When You Finally Stop Making Yourself the Center of Your Faith.
There is a kind of Christian exhaustion nobody talks about enough.
You wake up wanting to please God.
You promise yourself that today will be different.

You will pray more. Read your Bible. Control your thoughts. Resist temptation. Stop reacting in anger. Stop returning to that secret sin. Stop being the person you keep promising God you will never be again.
And for a while, you manage.
Then something happens.
An old temptation returns. A familiar wound gets touched. Your patience disappears. You say something you regret. You fall into something you thought you had already conquered.
And suddenly, there you are again.
Sitting in the silence.
Disappointed in yourself.
Wondering whether God is getting tired of hearing the same apology.
You open your Bible, but even the words seem to accuse you.
You try to pray, but shame has already started preaching its own sermon inside your head.
You should be stronger by now.
Real Christians don't keep struggling like this.
Maybe you were never serious about Jesus.
And without realizing it, your entire spiritual life becomes one long examination of yourself.
Your failures.
Your progress.
Your emotions.
Your weaknesses.
Your performance.
Your ability to remain faithful.
You are thinking about Christianity constantly.
But something is terribly wrong.
You are spending more time looking at the condition of your faith than looking at the Christ who is the foundation of your faith.
And Hebrews 12 has something to say to you.
Something far more beautiful than another command to try harder.
Something that could change the way you understand repentance, holiness, endurance, and the grace of God.
But before we reach it, there is a question you need to carry through this entire article.

What if the reason you are spiritually exhausted is not that you have been taking Jesus too seriously, but that you have been making yourself the center of a race that was always meant to be run with your eyes on Him?
Read that again.
Because there is a difference between examining your heart before God and making your heart the object of your hope.
And that difference matters more than you may realize.
Hebrews 12:1–2 says:

“Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,
Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God.”
— Hebrews 12:1–2, KJV
Notice something extraordinary.
The writer does not tell exhausted believers to run by staring at their feet.
He does not tell them to survive by obsessing over every stumble.
He does not tell them to become holy by making their own spiritual performance the center of their attention.
He tells them to lay aside sin, run with endurance, and look to Jesus.
And the original Greek makes this even more striking.
The expression translated “Looking unto Jesus” is:
ἀφορῶντες εἰς Ἰησοῦν
aphorōntes eis Iēsoun
The participle aphorōntes comes from the verb aphoraō, which carries the sense of directing one's gaze toward something, with the idea of looking away from other things.
It is not merely a passing glance.
It describes a deliberate orientation of attention.
The writer is calling believers to direct their gaze toward Jesus as they run.
This does not mean pretending that sin does not exist.
It does not mean refusing self-examination.
It does not mean ignoring the damage we have caused or avoiding the responsibility to repent.
After all, the very same passage commands us to throw off the sin that entangles us.
But it does mean that sin is something we must lay aside, while Jesus is the One upon whom our hope must rest.
Those are not the same thing.
And confusing them can turn the Christian life into a prison of endless self-occupation.
Think about Peter.
There was a night when he stepped out of a boat onto the Sea of Galilee.
The wind was real.
The waves were real.
The danger was real.
And Jesus was real.
Matthew 14 tells us that Peter walked on the water toward Jesus. But when he saw the strength of the wind, he became afraid and began to sink.
He cried out:
“Lord, save me.”
— Matthew 14:30, KJV
And what happened?
Jesus immediately stretched out His hand and caught him.
Not after Peter had proven that he deserved rescuing.
Not after Peter had successfully corrected his emotions.
Not after Peter had delivered a flawless explanation of his failure.
Immediately.
Now, Peter's experience is not a direct explanation of Hebrews 12, and we should not pretend the two passages teach precisely the same thing.
But there is a beautiful harmony between them.
Peter's rescue depended on the power of the Savior, not on Peter's ability to save himself.
And Christian endurance ultimately rests upon the faithfulness of Christ, not the illusion that we can make ourselves spiritually invincible.
Some of you have been trying to become stronger Christians by becoming harsher judges of yourselves.
You replay every mistake.
You interrogate every motive.
You measure your prayers.
You compare your spiritual growth with other believers.
You wonder why somebody else seems to have peace while you are still fighting battles nobody knows about.
And when you fall, you punish yourself with days of emotional distance from God.
As though remaining miserable long enough could somehow pay for what Jesus already carried to the cross.
But listen carefully.
Remorse is not the same as repentance. And self-punishment is not the same as holiness.
True repentance turns us away from sin and toward God.
It includes honest confession, a changed direction, and, where appropriate, making things right with those we have harmed.
But repentance does not require us to pretend that our suffering can add something to Christ's finished sacrifice.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Notice whose faithfulness is emphasized.
His.
Whose righteousness provides the foundation for forgiveness?
His.
Who cleanses?
He does.
You confess honestly.
You turn from sin.
You trust His promise.
And you continue following Jesus.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because the cross is sufficient.
There is a sentence in Hebrews 12:2 that deserves more attention than it often receives.
Jesus is described as:
τὸν τῆς πίστεως ἀρχηγὸν καὶ τελειωτὴν Ἰησοῦν
ton tēs pisteōs archēgon kai teleiōtēn Iēsoun
Jesus, the archēgos and teleiōtēs of faith.
The Greek word archēgos can describe a founder, pioneer, leader, or originator.
Teleiōtēs means one who brings something to its intended completion or perfection.
The KJV beautifully renders the expression “the author and finisher of our faith.”
Other translations speak of Jesus as the “founder and perfecter” or “pioneer and perfecter” of faith.
The original wording emphasizes Jesus' decisive place at the beginning and completion of the life of faith.
And here is why that matters.
The One you are looking toward is not merely a distant example shouting instructions from the finish line.
He is the crucified and risen Lord who has already endured the cross, conquered death, and taken His seat at the right hand of God.
The race is difficult.
The opposition is real.
The call to holiness is serious.
But the Christian does not run toward an uncertain Savior.
We run looking to the One who has already triumphed.
That changes everything.

Because many believers have quietly developed a version of Christianity in which Jesus saves them at the beginning, but afterward they imagine the entire burden rests upon their own spiritual strength.
They believe grace opened the door.
But now they must keep themselves inside through sheer determination.
So they live terrified.
Terrified of weakness.
Terrified of failure.
Terrified that one more stumble will reveal that God has finally had enough.
Yet the apostle Paul wrote:
“Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ.”
— Philippians 1:6, KJV
That promise is not permission for carelessness.
It is a reason for confidence in God's continuing work.
The same grace that saves us also trains us to reject ungodliness and live in a manner that honors Christ, as Titus 2:11–14 teaches.
Grace does not make holiness unnecessary.
Grace makes genuine holiness possible without turning holiness into a desperate attempt to purchase God's acceptance.
And perhaps that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Because some of you are not only fighting sin.
You are fighting memories.
You remember who you were before Christ.
The people you hurt.
The relationships you destroyed.
The lies you told.
The things you watched.
The compromises you made.
The moments when you knew what was right and chose what was wrong anyway.
You have asked God for forgiveness.
But every time you begin to experience peace, another memory appears.
And suddenly you feel guilty for being forgiven.
As though peace itself were an insult to the seriousness of your past.
You know the Bible says Jesus forgives.
You just struggle to believe that forgiveness could really include someone who has done what you have done.
And here is where the Gospel becomes almost unbearably beautiful.
Jesus does not redeem imaginary sinners.
He redeems real ones.
People with histories.
People with regrets.
People whose sins were not misunderstandings.
People who cannot travel backward and undo what they did.
The apostle Paul knew something about that.
Before his conversion, he persecuted the church.
He was not merely confused about a minor theological disagreement.
He was actively opposing the people of Christ.
Yet Paul later wrote:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.”
— 1 Timothy 1:15, KJV
Paul did not erase the truth about his past.
He remembered it honestly.
But his past no longer had the final word over his identity and mission.
The mercy of Jesus did.
And that is the scandal of grace.
Not that sin suddenly becomes harmless.
Not that consequences disappear.
Not that repentance becomes optional.
But that Jesus Christ can take someone whose life bears the evidence of rebellion and transform that person into a living testimony of divine mercy.
Your past may explain some of your scars, but it does not possess the authority to overrule what Christ has accomplished for those who belong to Him.
Not because the scandal was small.
But because the Savior is greater.
And yet there is another danger we must confront.
Because someone could read all of this and conclude that looking to Jesus means never examining ourselves.
That would be a serious misunderstanding.
Scripture commands self-examination.
Second Corinthians 13:5 tells believers to examine themselves concerning the faith.
Psalm 139:23–24 models a prayer for God to search the heart and expose wickedness.
James 1:22 warns against hearing God's Word without obeying it.
And Hebrews 12 itself calls us to lay aside every weight and the sin that so easily entangles us.
The Christian life is not spiritual denial.
We cannot simply say, “I am looking at Jesus,” while deliberately protecting the sin for which He died.
But there is an enormous difference between examining ourselves in the light of Christ and examining ourselves as though we were our own saviors.
Healthy self-examination asks:
Lord, what must I confess?
What must I surrender?
Whom have I wounded?
Where am I resisting Your Word?
How can I obey You today?
Destructive self-occupation keeps asking:
Am I good enough yet?
Have I finally become impressive enough?
Why am I not as strong as everyone else?
How can I make myself worthy of being loved?
One leads us toward humble repentance and renewed obedience.
The other can trap us in an endless cycle of spiritual self-measurement.
And the Gospel answers that second kind of questioning with a crucified Savior.
You do not become worthy of grace by reaching a level of personal perfection.
You receive grace because Jesus is merciful.
And that grace begins changing how you live.
Consider the words of Hebrews 12:3:
“For consider him that endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, lest ye be wearied and faint in your minds.”
— Hebrews 12:3, KJV
There it is again.
Consider Him.
The Greek verb is ἀναλογίσασθε (analogisasthe).
It calls for thoughtful, careful consideration.
The writer is not telling weary Christians to stop thinking.
He is telling them where to direct their thinking.
Consider Jesus.
Think deeply about His endurance.
Remember the hostility He suffered.
Remember His obedience.
Remember the cross.
Remember that He did not turn away from the Father's will when suffering became unbearable.
Why?
So that you do not grow weary and lose heart.
Hebrews 12 was written to people who needed endurance in the face of real hardship and opposition.
Its primary concern is not simply the private emotional struggle of an individual believer.
It is a call for God's people to persevere faithfully.
That context matters.
Because the passage does not promise that fixing our eyes on Jesus will remove every hardship.
It promises something deeper through its exhortation.
A worthy focus for endurance.
A Savior whose suffering and triumph give believers reason to keep running.
And this brings us to a truth that may be difficult to hear.
Sometimes the Christian life hurts.
Not because God has abandoned you.
Not necessarily because you have done something wrong.
And not because every painful experience is a punishment for some hidden sin.
Hebrews 12 goes on to discuss the Father's discipline of His children.
The Greek word παιδεία (paideia) refers to training, education, or discipline.
The passage portrays God's fatherly discipline as purposeful, directed toward holiness and the peaceful fruit of righteousness.
It does not give us permission to label every tragedy as a direct correction from God.
Nor does it excuse cruelty or abuse by calling them divine discipline.
But it does remind believers that the Father is committed to forming His children.
And growth can involve correction.
Surrender can be painful.
Learning to forgive may take time.
Breaking destructive habits may require confession, accountability, wise counsel, and difficult changes.
Faithfulness may mean refusing a temptation that once felt like comfort.
It may mean apologizing when pride wants to defend itself.
It may mean walking away from a relationship that keeps pulling you into sin.
It may mean continuing to obey Jesus when nobody applauds.
And sometimes, after doing everything you know to do, you will still feel weak.
That does not automatically mean your faith has failed.
It may simply mean you are discovering what it means to depend on Christ rather than pretending you are sufficient in yourself.
Paul heard the Lord say:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.”
— 2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
That verse does not glorify sin.
It glorifies the sufficiency of Christ amid human weakness.
There is a difference.
And for the believer who has spent years believing that weakness makes them useless to God, that difference is life-changing.
You do not have to pretend to be strong in order to come to Jesus.
You do have to come honestly.
And you must be willing to follow Him.
Maybe you are reading this after another failure.
Maybe you have been hiding a struggle because you are terrified of what people in church would think.
Maybe your marriage is hurting.
Maybe you have been spiritually numb for months.
Maybe you serve in ministry, encourage everybody else, quote Scripture publicly, and then go home wondering why your own heart feels so empty.
Maybe you have confused being busy for God with actually abiding in Christ.
And perhaps the most painful possibility is this:
You have spent so much time trying to prove that you are a faithful Christian that you have forgotten the joy of simply belonging to Jesus.
Listen to His invitation.
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
— Matthew 11:28, KJV
He did not say, “Come when you have finally become impressive.”
He did not say, “Come when your history is spotless.”
He did not say, “Come when you can guarantee that you will never struggle again.”
He said, “Come unto me.”
And the rest He offers is not a promise that discipleship will require nothing.
The following verses speak of taking His yoke and learning from Him.
His invitation is to a new way of life under His gracious lordship.
Not independence from Him.
Dependence upon Him.
That is why fixing our eyes on Jesus is not an excuse to become passive.
It is the foundation for faithful action.
You confess because He is faithful.
You repent because He is worthy.
You forgive because you have received mercy.
You resist sin because you belong to Him.
You pursue holiness because grace has begun transforming you.
You endure because the One who calls you is faithful.
And when you stumble, you do not build a home in the dust.
You turn again to Christ.
You receive His correction.
You seek the help you need.
You get back into the race.
Not boasting in your strength.
Not excusing your sin.
But trusting the Savior who is worthy of your gaze.
And now we come to one of the most breathtaking details in Hebrews 12:2.
Jesus endured the cross:
ἀντὶ τῆς προκειμένης αὐτῷ χαρᾶς
anti tēs prokeimenēs autō charas
The expression is commonly translated “for the joy that was set before him.”

The preposition anti can carry different senses depending on context, including “for the sake of” or “in place of.” In this passage, the traditional rendering emphasizes the joy set before Jesus in connection with His endurance.
The text does not identify that joy in a single explanatory sentence.
But within the larger New Testament witness, Christ's obedience, His exaltation, and the saving purpose of His work illuminate the hope bound up with His suffering.
He endured the cross.
He despised its shame.
And He sat down at the right hand of God's throne.
Think about that.
The cross was an instrument of public humiliation.
It was designed to expose, degrade, and destroy.
And Jesus endured it.
The sinless Son of God entered the deepest humiliation of crucifixion.
Not because He deserved punishment for His own wrongdoing.
But because, as the Scriptures teach, He gave Himself for sinners.
First Peter 3:18 says:
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God.”
That he might bring us to God.
Do not rush past those words.
The Gospel is not merely about becoming a better version of yourself.
It is about being reconciled to the God from whom sin has separated us.
It is about forgiveness purchased at a cost we could never pay.
It is about a Savior who died and rose again.
It is about receiving a new life that cannot be explained by self-improvement alone.
And if Jesus endured the shame of the cross to bring sinners to God, why would we imagine that the answer to spiritual exhaustion is to make our own shame the center of our attention?
The cross does not teach us to ignore our guilt.
It teaches us where guilt must be brought.
To Jesus.
The One who can forgive.
The One who can cleanse.
The One who can restore.
The One who can transform.
This is why the words “From Scandal to Grace” are more than a memorable phrase for Gospel Warrior.
They describe the astonishing direction of redemption.
From rebellion to repentance.
From condemnation to justification in Christ.
From slavery to sin toward a life of obedience.
From spiritual death to life in the risen Savior.
Not every broken relationship will be restored exactly as it was.
Not every earthly consequence will disappear.
Not every painful memory will vanish.
But in Christ, sin and shame need not have the final word.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the old story never happened.
But by bringing forgiven sinners into a new story of grace, truth, and transformation.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to stop right here.
Not to make another dramatic promise about how perfect tomorrow will be.
Not to bargain with God.
Not to manufacture an emotional experience.
But simply to pray honestly.
“Lord Jesus, I have been looking at myself more than I have been looking at You.
I have allowed my failures to become louder than Your promises.
I have sometimes confused shame with repentance and self-condemnation with holiness.
Search my heart.
Expose what I need to confess.
Give me courage to turn away from sin.
Teach me to trust Your finished work.
Help me obey You, not to earn Your love, but because You have shown such great mercy.
When I become weary, remind me to consider You.
When I stumble, lead me back to repentance.
When I grow proud, humble me.
When I despair, remind me of Your grace.
Fix my eyes on You, Jesus.
Not on the Christian I am pretending to be.
Not on the Christian I wish I had already become.
But on You, my Savior, my Lord, and my hope.
Amen.”
And if that prayer describes something you have been carrying quietly, I want to invite you into an honest conversation.
You do not have to reveal private details publicly.
You do not have to perform vulnerability for an audience.
But perhaps your simple testimony will remind another struggling believer that they are not the only one learning to depend on grace.
And if you need prayer, you can simply comment, “Pray for me.”
There are people reading these words who may be fighting battles no one else can see.
Let us become the kind of Christian community where truth is spoken without cruelty, repentance is encouraged without humiliation, and grace is celebrated without compromising holiness.
Because discipleship was never meant to be a competition over who looks the strongest.
We are people who need Jesus.
Every one of us.
And if this message has helped you understand Hebrews 12 more clearly, please do not let it end with you.
Someone in your family may be quietly drowning in religious guilt.
A friend may be ready to walk away from faith because they believe their failures have made them beyond redemption.
A believer who appears spiritually strong may be exhausted from years of trying to earn what Christ freely gives.
And someone who does not yet know Jesus may need to discover that Christianity is not merely a system of moral improvement, but the good news of salvation through the crucified and risen Son of God.
Return to Hebrews 12:1–3.
Read the passage in context.
Remember the witnesses of faith in Hebrews 11.
Remember the call to lay aside sin.
Remember the command to endure.
And above all, remember the One toward whom the passage directs your eyes.
Jesus.
And invite your family, your friends, the believer who has grown distant, the seeker asking honest questions, and even the person who is not yet convinced about Christianity.
Let them encounter the Scriptures.
Let them consider the claims of Jesus.
Let them see that the Christian faith has room for honest questions, serious repentance, patient discipleship, and the transforming mercy of God.
Not because God's favor can be purchased.
Biblical giving is not supposed to be driven by guilt or pressure.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should be willing, not reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
And while Christians hold differing convictions about the application of tithing under the New Covenant, Scripture clearly encourages generosity and the support of worthwhile ministry.
Your generosity can help us continue the work and reach more people with Scripture-centered encouragement.
These products are not the Gospel, and buying them is not a measure of devotion to Christ.
Our desire is to make biblical nourishment, spiritual encouragement, and discipleship resources accessible to as many people as possible.
You are not purchasing a place in God's family.
You are not buying a blessing.
You are not earning forgiveness.
And your value before God is not measured by the amount you can give.
The Gospel remains the Gospel.
Salvation is by grace through faith in Christ, not a reward for financial support.
And that truth is too precious to compromise.
The exhausted Christian.
The one sitting alone after another failure.
The one who cannot stop replaying the past.
The one who keeps promising God that tomorrow will be different.
Maybe that person is you.
And maybe tonight, for the first time in a long time, you can approach God without pretending.
You can confess what is wrong.
You can stop defending what needs to change.
You can seek forgiveness where you have caused harm.
You can ask for help with the sin that keeps entangling you.
And you can stop believing that staring at your brokenness will somehow make you whole.
Because Hebrews 12 does not call you to deny the race.
It does not call you to ignore the obstacles.
It does not call you to celebrate sin.
It calls you to run.
With endurance.
Laying aside what entangles you.
And looking to Jesus.
The Author and Finisher.
The crucified and risen Savior.
The One who endured the cross.
The One who is seated at the right hand of God.
The One who is worthy of your faith.
So when tomorrow comes, and the old voices begin again...
When shame tells you to hide...
When pride tells you to prove yourself...
When fear tells you that you will never change...
When temptation tells you that surrender is pointless...
Remember where Scripture directs your gaze.
Not inward as though your strength were sufficient.
Not backward as though your past were sovereign.
Not sideways as though another believer's progress determined your worth.
But toward Jesus Christ.
And as you look to Him, keep obeying.
Keep repenting.
Keep trusting.
Keep running.
Not because the road will always be easy.
But because the Savior is worthy.
And because the One who endured the cross is infinitely more deserving of your attention than the shame that keeps demanding it.
You were never meant to spend your whole life staring at the chains Jesus came to break while forgetting to look at the Savior who holds the key.
